title: The stories hiding in old photos: an album afternoon
description: A box of old family photos is an archive with no index — the names and stories live only in people's memories. One afternoon with an older relative and a pencil can rescue them before they fade.

body.heading: Photos remember less than people do
paragraphs: A photograph preserves faces and places but not names, jokes, or why everyone is laughing. Within a generation or two, most family photos become pictures of strangers: the people are recognisable as relatives and unknowable as people. The knowledge of who they were exists in exactly one place — the memory of the oldest person who knew them.

That makes an album afternoon a rescue mission disguised as a visit. Spread the photos out, choose the ones nobody can name, and let the oldest relative talk. Their identifications — 'that's your great-grandfather's brother, the one who kept bees' — are the captions the album never had.

body.heading: Write it down, gently
paragraphs: Write names and dates in pencil on the back of prints, or keep a numbered list beside the box: photo 12, front left, name, one remembered detail. One detail matters — 'kept bees' turns a stranger back into a person faster than a full biography.

Go slowly and let the stories wander; the detours are usually the treasure. And record the session if they are willing, because a voice saying 'that's your great-grandfather' is itself an heirloom now.

takeaway: Old photos keep faces but lose names and stories within a generation — an afternoon labelling them with an older relative, one remembered detail at a time, rescues the family's memory.
